title: Quarto presentations
text:
Contributions
You are welcome to add new presentations or improve the current ones. The guidelines for contributors are explained here. The presentations are deployed from the quarto sub-directory, so you need to make the respective changes there and run cd quarto/; quarto render.
The following is a quick workflow for contributions:

fork the repository
add your qmd file(s) to the quarto sub-directory
update the _quarto.yml file and the list of presentations in the website with the name of the qmd file(s) with your presentation(s)
run quarto render, or in R quarto::quarto_render(myfilename) from your terminal from within the quarto sub-directory
and make a pull request to the master branch

This documentation provides more details about publishing quarto presentations with GitHub Pages.

title: Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis with Bioconductor

Data containers are in core


In Bioconductor, the core of software is formed by data containers.
When we agree with the data format, developers can develop interoperable methods and packages that then the users can utilize to analyze their data.

title: Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis with Bioconductor
text:
SummarizedExperiment
(Huber et al. 2015)


SummarizedExperiment was develop for generic data container for biological data analysis.
Nowadays, it is the main data container adpoted by many fields.
Genomics, metabolomics, …

title: Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis with Bioconductor
text:
TreeSummarizedExperiment
(Huang et al. 2021)


Microbiome field was using different data container. It is like dancing the disco dance alone while others are dancing in the dance floor. If you are Zulip (you should), you can find a video of disco dance instructions.
So Huang and others extended this SummarizedExperimet class to support trees which is a typical format to present bacterial phylogeny trees.

Building the microbiome community in Bioconductor

Common data standard TreeSummarizedExperiment
Interoperable software (methods from international community)
Shared knowledge (online book)
Open collaboration


We now have the infrastructure, methods, and documentation.
The next challenge is not technical.
The challenge is building a community where developers, researchers, and users work together on common standards and interoperable tools.
Something that I look up is the tidyomics community. They have been very successful building their community, and I want that microbiome will have something similar in the future.

title: Orchestrating Hologenome Analysis with Bioconductor
text:
Mantel test
Question: Are two omics datasets related?

Compares distance matrices
Tests for a global association between omics layers


The Mantel test asks whether samples that are similar in one omics dataset are also similar in another.

title: Orchestrating Hologenome Analysis with Bioconductor
text:
Microbiome Regression-based Kernel Association Test (MiRKAT)
Question: Is a pathway associated with the global microbiome profile?

Represents microbiome similarity between samples
Tests its association with a pathway


MiRKAT uses a kernel to represent similarity between microbiome profiles. It therefore tests the microbiome at a global level rather than testing individual taxa.

title: Orchestrating Hologenome Analysis with Bioconductor
text:
Pairwise association
Question: Which features are associated?

Tests feature–feature associations
Can reveal candidate biological interactions


Rather than asking whether the two datasets are globally related, pairwise methods identify specific associations between features.
Limitation: pairwise associations consider features individually and do not account for the role of microbes within the broader microbial network.

title: Orchestrating Hologenome Analysis with Bioconductor
section: Joint robust principal component analysis (joint RPCA) (Cordazzo Vargas et al. 2026)
text:
Joint robust principal component analysis (joint RPCA) (Cordazzo Vargas et al. 2026)
Question: What are the main shared patterns?

Denoise: learn a lower-dimensional representation (samples × dimensions)
PCA: find components that capture maximum variance
Visualize: samples in PCA space and identify the loadings driving the variation


Joint RPCA first denoises each data layer by approximating it in a lower dimensional space, allowing layer-specific weights. The resulting representations are then combined and PCA is applied to obtain a shared low-dimensional space. A scatter plot can then be used to visualize how samples relate across the integrated omics data.

title: Orchestrating Hologenomic Analysis with Bioconductor
text:
Early fusion
Combine first
Concatenate omics tables into a single feature matrix and train one model.

Intermediate fusion
Learn first
Train separate models for each omics layer, then combine their learned representations.

Late fusion
Predict first
Train separate models for each omics layer, then combine their predictions.

title: Orchestrating Hologenome Analysis with Bioconductor
text:
Other approaches

Anansi tests biologically informed pairwise associations (Bastiaanssen, Quinn, and Cryan 2023).
Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA) finds shared and layer-specific latent factors (Argelaguet et al. 2020).
DIABLO, implemented in mixOmics, identifies multi-omics features that discriminate groups (Rohart et al. 2017).

title: Orchestrating Hologenome Analysis with Bioconductor
text:
Multi-omics data fusion





Early fusion: Concatenate the different data tables into a single table and train one machine-learning model on the combined features.
Intermediate fusion: Train separate models for each omics layer and then use a meta-model to combine the information or predictions from these models. This approach can often capture complementary information more flexibly than simple early or late fusion.
Late fusion: Train a separate model for each omics layer and combine their predictions, for example by averaging or weighting them.

title: Bioconductor
text:
Related ecosystems


Over the years, several approaches to data organization have been developed. One of the first widely adopted data containers in microbiome research was phyloseq (McMurdie and Holmes 2013), designed for 16S amplicon sequencing data. However, it has limitations, particularly in linking multiple experiments and ensuring interoperability between tools in Bioconductor.
SummarizedExperiment (SE) (Huber et al. 2015), on the other hand, was introduced as a general-purpose container for biological data and has become the most widely used format within the Bioconductor ecosystem. It has since been extended to more specialized formats, including SingleCellExperiment (Amezquita et al. 2020) for single-cell data and TreeSummarizedExperiment (TreeSE) (Huang et al. 2021), which is tailored for microbiome datasets.

title: Bioconductor
section: Benefits of a shared data framework
text:
Benefits of a shared data framework

Tightly linked with broader Bioconductor ecosystem
Improved scalability
Improved multi-table integration



We use same data format as broader Bioconductor ecosystem. Some of you might know phyloseq. That was specifically designed for 16S amplicon data, and is not supported outside its ecosystem. Moreover, microbiome data science is nowadays more than sequencing data, it links different fields from metabolomics to genomics. Same data format allows us to use methods from different fields.
The ecosystem is more scalable; speed and memory wise than phyloseq and its more efficient alternative, speedyseq. It is not uncommon anymore that there are tens of thousands of samples and features so we need efficient software to run these big datasets.
This ecosystem allows us to link multiple tables together, facilitating multi-omics integration by supporting management of this kind of complex datasets.

📓
Reproducible

📚

title: Microbiome data science workflow
text:
Setup

library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(scater)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(1)  # reproducible permutation tests

# Example data set: skin microbiome with sample metadata
data("peerj13075", package = "mia")
tse <- peerj13075

# Relative abundances and CLR for downstream steps
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "clr", pseudocount = TRUE)

# Genus-level summary
tse_genus <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "genus")


The workflow operates on a TreeSummarizedExperiment. Replace the example data with your own.

text:
Alpha diversity: within-sample


Tasks

Estimate alpha diversity per sample
Draw a histogram
Compare two or more indices, visually and/or statistically



tse <- addAlpha(
    tse, index = c("shannon", "observed"))

p1 <- plotHistogram(
    tse, col.var = "shannon", bins = 15)
p2 <- plotColData(
    tse, x = "observed", y = "shannon")
p1 + p2

Do richness and evenness agree? Here Spearman \(\rho\) = 0.43.

Beta diversity: community variation
Visualize community variation with PCoA, and check how the data transformation affects it:


Bray–Curtis
on compositional (relative abundance) data


Euclidean
on CLR-transformed data (Aitchison distance)



tse <- runMDS(tse, FUN = getDissimilarity, method = "bray",
              assay.type = "relabundance", name = "PCoA_BC")
tse <- runMDS(tse, FUN = getDissimilarity, method = "euclidean",
              assay.type = "clr", name = "PCoA_CLR")

plotReducedDim(tse, "PCoA_BC",  colour_by = "Diet")
plotReducedDim(tse, "PCoA_CLR", colour_by = "Diet")

title: Microbiome data science workflow
text:
Community-level comparisons
Does community composition differ between groups?



PERMANOVA tests group differences in composition
Add covariates (e.g. age, sex) and see how the results change
Check homogeneity of dispersion



res <- getPERMANOVA(
    tse,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    method = "bray",
    formula = x ~ Geographical_location + Gender + Age,
    test.homogeneity = TRUE)

res$permanova |>
    knitr::kable(digits = 3)




PERMANOVA is sensitive to differences in group spread (dispersion), not only location, so check homogeneity of dispersion alongside the test (res$homogeneity).

title: Microbiome data science workflow
text:
Prevalence
What is the most prevalent genus in the data?

prev <- getPrevalence(
    tse_genus, assay.type = "relabundance",
    detection = 0, sort = TRUE)
round(head(prev, 4), 2)

 Staphylococcus   Paenibacillus        Bacillus Corynebacterium 
           1.00            1.00            1.00            0.93 


prevalence = fraction of samples where a taxon is detected above a given abundance threshold

title: Microbiome data science workflow
text:
Core microbiota
Taxa above 0.1 % relative abundance in over 50 % of samples (Salonen et al. 2012). How sensitive is this to the thresholds?


core <- getPrevalent(
    tse_genus,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    detection = 0.1 / 100,
    prevalence = 50 / 100)

plotAbundanceDensity(
    tse_genus[core, ],
    layout = "jitter",
    assay.type = "relabundance")

title: Microbiome data science workflow
text:
Differential abundance
Which genera are associated with a group difference (e.g. sex)?

library(DESeq2)

dds <- DESeqDataSet(tse_genus, design = ~ Gender)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds)

top <- head(res[order(res$padj), ])
data.frame(log2FC = round(top$log2FoldChange, 2),
           padj = signif(top$padj, 2),
           row.names = rownames(top)) |>
    knitr::kable()



DESeq2 (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014); for alternatives and benchmarks see the OMA DAA chapter
Compare several methods: results can differ substantially

title: Microbiome data science workflow
text:
Role of covariates

Key covariates (diet, medication, age, …) can change the interpretation.


Stool consistency, medication and diet explain a considerable part of population-level gut microbiome variation (Falony et al. 2016)
Include relevant covariates in PERMANOVA and differential abundance models
Compare results with and without covariates

title: Agglomeration
text:
Why agglomerate?

Focus on biologically meaningful units
Reduce sparsity and noise
Improve interpretability of downstream analyses



Focusing on higher-level taxa (e.g., genera instead of thousands of ASVs) helps highlight biologically relevant patterns.
16S sequencing often does not resolve taxa below genus level reliably.
Agglomeration reduces noise from sequencing artifacts and rare features.
Makes downstream analyses like diversity metrics, ordination, and association studies more interpretable.
Note: Some resolution is lost when collapsing features—balance simplicity with detail.

title: Agglomeration
text:
Summing up the taxonomy


Counts of species belonging to the same genus are summed up: Genus A gets 3 + 5 + 4 = 12.

title: Agglomeration
text:
Example data
Colorectal cancer gut metagenomes (Gupta et al. 2019)

Data and import script: github.com/microbiome/data


library(mia)
library(ape)

read <- function(f) read.csv(file.path("GuptaA_2019", f), row.names = 1)

tse <- TreeSummarizedExperiment(
    assays  = list(counts = as.matrix(read("taxonomy_abundance.csv"))),
    rowData = read("taxonomy_table.csv"),
    colData = read("sample_metadata.csv"),
    rowTree = read.tree("GuptaA_2019/phylogeny.tree")
)


The demonstration below uses the GlobalPatterns data set that ships with mia, so it runs without downloads.

title: Agglomeration
text: Demonstration

title: Agglomeration
text:
Agglomerate to one rank

library(mia)
data("GlobalPatterns", package = "mia")
tse <- GlobalPatterns

tse_phylum <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "Phylum")
c(features = nrow(tse), phyla = nrow(tse_phylum))

features    phyla 
   19216       66 



19,216 features collapse to 66 phyla. Assays are summed and rowData is trimmed to the ranks at and above phylum.

tse <- agglomerateByRanks(tse)
sapply(altExps(tse), nrow)

title: Transformation
text:
Microbiome data

High variability: feature abundances vary widely across samples
Zero-inflation: many taxa absent in most samples
Compositionality: only relative abundances observed; total counts per sample are arbitrary



High variability → lots of variation in abundances
Zero-inflation → many features are absent in most samples, which complicates statistical modelling and increases sparsity of the data matrix.
Compositionality → sequencing depth differs between samples; only ratios of features within a sample are meaningful, absolute counts are not.

title: Transformation
text:
Heteroscedasticity


Heteroscedasticity: the variance increases with the mean. Abundant taxa have lots of variability.

title: Transformation
text:
Zero-inflation


Real microbiome data. Lots of zeroes.

title: Transformation
text:
Compositionality

Sequencing measures relative abundances, not true microbial counts
Values are parts of a whole
Parts are linked by a fixed total (library size)

If one increases, at least one other must decrease



Sequencing does not measure the true number of bacteria in a sample. Each sample produces an arbitrary total number of reads (library size) due to technical variation and bias.
Because all microbes share this fixed total, we observe only relative abundances, not absolute quantities.
Most standard statistical methods assume variables can change independently. Compositional data violate this assumption: all values must sum to the same total, so changes are always relative.
Ignoring this constraint can lead to misleading results, even when the data look reasonable.
Everyday examples of compositional data include: - A budget - How you spend 24 hours in a day (more work means less time for something else)

title: Transformation
text:
Same counts, different proportions


These plots show the same two samples in two different ways.
On the left, we see absolute counts. Taxon A increases in Sample 2, while taxa B and C stay exactly the same.
On the right, we see relative abundances, which is what sequencing gives us. Because each sample has a fixed library size, all taxa must share the same total.
As taxon A takes up a larger share in Sample 2, the proportions of B and C go down — even though their true counts did not change.
This is compositional bias: changes in one taxon can make others appear to change simply because everything is expressed as proportions.

title: Transformation
text:
Compositionality is not optional

“… microbiome datasets generated by HTS are compositional because they have an arbitrary total imposed by the instrument.”


“… HTS datasets derived from microbiome studies can and should be treated as compositions at all stages of analysis.”



Quoted from the abstract of Gloor et al. (2017). HTS = high-throughput sequencing.


Gloor et al. (2017), Microbiome datasets are compositional: and this is not optional

title: Transformation
text:
Goals of transformation

Mitigate biases in abundances
Make features comparable across samples
Meet assumptions of downstream statistical analyses



Transformations allow standard analyses like PCA, regression, correlation.
Choose transformation depending on the problem: relative abundance, log, CLR, etc.

title: Transformation
text:
Relative abundance

Library sizes are arbitrary

\[
\text{X}_{ij} = \frac{\text{Count}_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^m \text{Count}_{ik}}
\]
where

\(i\) indexes the sample,
\(j\) indexes the taxon,
\(m\) is the total number of taxa.


Library sizes were arbitrary –> remove their effect.

Library sizes differ between samples (sequencing depth varies), so raw counts are not directly comparable.
Relative abundance converts counts to proportions within each sample, making samples comparable.
Intuition: a relative abundance of 0.2 means “this taxon makes up 20% of this sample,” independent of total reads.

title: Transformation
text:
Log-transformed relative abundance

Library sizes are arbitrary and data zero-inflated

\[
\text{X}_{ij} = \log \left( \text{Relative abundance}_{ij} + \epsilon \right)
\]
where

\(\epsilon\) is a small pseudocount to avoid \(\log(0)\).


Zero-inflated –> reduce the data skewness
Log-transform reduces skewness and makes differences among low-abundance taxa more visible, but a pseudocount is required to handle zeros.

title: Transformation
text:
Counts, proportions, logs


The data is still constrained to relative abundances (0-1), but now in log-scale.
Because the total is fixed, the numbers depend on each other.
If one goes up, at least one of the others must go down. This is called a constraint.

title: Transformation
text:
Centered log-ratio (CLR)

Library sizes are arbitrary and values are dependent

\[
\text{CLR}(x_i) = \log\left(\frac{x_i}{g(x)}\right),\quad
g(x) = \left(\prod_{j=1}^{D} x_j \right)^{1/D}
\]

\(x_i\): abundance of bacteria \(i\)
\(g(x)\): geometric mean across all bacteria in the sample


CLR is a standard transformation for compositional data. It accounts for dependency between parts and arbitrary library sizes, which simple relative abundance transformations cannot.

title: Transformation
text:
Intuition

Values dependent, only ratios matter


This is the idea behind CLR transformation.
When we want to compare values in compositional data, only ratios make sense.

title: Transformation
text:
Intuition

Values dependent, only ratios matter
Standard statistics rely on subtraction and distance


However, most statistical tests rely on subtraction making sense. How to turn ratios into differences?

title: Transformation
text:
Intuition

Values dependent, only ratios matter
Standard statistics rely on subtraction and distance

\[
\frac{x}{y} \;\longrightarrow\; a - b \;?
\]

This is the situation.

title: Transformation
text:
Intuition

Values dependent, only ratios matter
Standard statistics rely on subtraction and distance

Use log-scale


\[
\log\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = \log(x) - \log(y)
\]

Taking the log turns multiplicative relationships (ratios) into additive ones (differences), making subtraction meaningful.

title: Transformation
text:
Intuition

Values dependent, only ratios matter
Standard statistics rely on subtraction and distance

Use log-scale

Library sizes are arbitrary


Library sizes are arbitrary. This means that the scale of values are arbitrary. How to remove the effect of them?

title: Transformation
text:
Intuition

Values dependent, only ratios matter
Standard statistics rely on subtraction and distance

Use log-scale

Library sizes are arbitrary

Center the data



By centering the data, i.e., removing the mean.

title: Transformation
text:
Centering


Centering means that we subtract mean from each value to get the distribution centered to 0. Because we use log-scale, we have to use suitable mean (geometric mean aka arithmetic mean in log-scale).

title: Transformation
text:
Centering the logs
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{CLR}(x_i) &= \log\left(\frac{x_i}{g(x)}\right) \\[2mm]
&= \log(x_i) - \log(g(x))
\end{aligned}
\]

We remove the mean.
Why we remove geometric mean?

title: Transformation
text:
Why the geometric mean?
\[
\text{Arithmetic mean} = \frac{2 + 8 + 32}{3} = \frac{42}{3} = 14
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Geometric mean} &= \sqrt[3]{2 \cdot 8 \cdot 32} \\[2mm]
&= \exp\left( \frac{\log 2 + \log 8 + \log 32}{3} \right) \\[2mm]
&= 8
\end{aligned}
\]

The geometric mean is just the arithmetic mean in log-space. Because now the values are in logarithmic space, we have to use geometric mean.

title: Transformation
text:
Intuition: summary

Values dependent, only ratios matter
Standard statistics rely on subtraction and distance

Use log-scale

Library sizes are arbitrary

Center the data



CLR converts compositional data into a format where subtraction, distances, and correlations make sense. This solves both the dependency and library size issues.

title: Transformation
text:
Centered log-ratio (CLR)
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{CLR}(x_i) &= \log\left(\frac{x_i}{g(x)}\right) \\[2mm]
&= \log(x_i) - \log(g(x)) \\[2mm]
&= \log(x_i) - \frac{1}{D}\sum_{j=1}^{D}\log(x_j)
\end{aligned}
\]


Take a logarithm of the values –> ratios become subtraction which is what we want in Euclidean space
Center values to mean 0
CLR values show how each feature compares to the sample’s geometric mean.
Positive = enriched, Negative = depleted.
Magnitude gives a fold-change interpretation on a log scale.

title: Transformation
text:
CLR in practice

Removes compositional constraints (constant sum)
Values centered around zero, symmetric
Allows standard statistical tools (PCA, correlations)
Debate on whether it is necessary in DA



CLR is widely used in microbiome data analysis because it removes compositional constraints and often makes data more normally distributed.
However, recent benchmark studies highlight some limitations in differential abundance (DA) analysis:

Can lack sensitivity
May produce paradoxical results in low-diversity microbiomes

CLR values are harder to interpret than relative abundances because each value is dependent on the other features in the sample

Despite this, CLR remains a standard, especially for methods that assume Euclidean space.

title: Transformation
text:
Counts versus CLR


Makes the data more normally distributed. Distributed around zero. Without constrains (goes from negative infinity to positive)

title: Transformation
text:
Correct transformation depends on

Your research question
The analysis method


Use the simplest justified approach that works


There is increasing amount of benchmarking literature on this. We combine them to online book.
The “best” transformation depends on what you want to learn and the statistical methods you plan to use. Often, a simple, well-justified approach works well in practice.

title: Transformation
text:
Demonstration

library(mia)
data("GlobalPatterns", package = "mia")
tse <- GlobalPatterns

tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "clr", pseudocount = TRUE)
assayNames(tse)

title: Transformation
text:
Absolute versus relative


These plots show the same two samples in two different ways.
On the left, we see absolute counts. Taxon A increases in Sample 2, while taxa B and C stay exactly the same.
On the right, we see relative abundances, which is what sequencing gives us. Because each sample has a fixed library size, all taxa must share the same total.
As taxon A takes up a larger share in Sample 2, the proportions of B and C go down — even though their true counts did not change.
This is compositional bias: changes in one taxon can make others appear to change simply because everything is expressed as proportions.

title: Transformation
text:
Relative versus quantitative profiling







The same samples profiled in two ways. On the left, relative abundances (RMP): every sample sums to 100 %. On the right, quantitative abundances (QMP): relative profiles scaled by the microbial cell count per gram, measured with flow cytometry. Microbial load varies several-fold between samples, which the relative profile hides entirely.


RMP: relative microbiome profiling; QMP: quantitative microbiome profiling. Vandeputte et al. (2017)

title: Transformation
section: RMP vs. QMP: conclusions can flip
text:
RMP vs. QMP: conclusions can flip







Crohn’s disease (CD) patients have lower microbial loads (a). With relative profiling, Bacteroides appears enriched in CD; with quantitative profiling, that difference disappears, whereas Prevotella is significantly depleted in CD only under QMP (b).
Potentially drastic effect on conclusions!


Vandeputte et al. (2017)
